name: PT Jakarta International Hotels & Development Tbk

frontmatter.title: Jakarta International Hotels & Development: a trough-earnings DCF at a discount to parent book
frontmatter.summary: JIHD trades far below parent book while revenue has stabilised and Jakarta hotel occupancy is improving. Our HOLD and target of Rp320 rest on a DCF that values a slow cyclical recovery, after the 20.0% liquidity discount; the shares already sit close to that value. The P/BV cross-check is shown at today's multiple, not the own-history mean, because no source supports a re-rating. A controller-dominated register, a thin free float and a loss-making operating base are the constraints.
thesis: The shares trade at 0.2x parent book value while the September 2026 balance sheet holds net cash and IDR1,452.6bn of equity-method investments [S3]; the target is DCF-led, not an asset revaluation.

Revenue was flat in FY2025A at IDR1,612.9bn and grew only slightly in the first nine months of FY2026 [S3], while Jakarta star-hotel occupancy of 58.2% in September 2026 and arrivals of 12.0 m visits point to a gradual recovery that supports our growth path [S4, S6].

Operating costs, not gross margin, drove the FY2025A loss: a real-estate G&A step-up took opex to IDR1,486.9bn, and our base case assumes only partial normalisation, so EBITDA stays thin through the forecast [S2].

The target is DCF-led: the primary DCF carries 80% and a no-terminal-value life DCF at 20% sits -24.3% below it; P/BV is a cross-check only, because at today's 0.2x parent book it values the shares close to the DCF, while the own-history mean would require a near-doubling of the multiple that no source supports. A liquidity discount of 20.0% is applied for a 24.5% free float [S0].
Related-party flows are large but stable, chiefly cash at the affiliated Bank Artha Graha and rent from Electronic City, and no manipulation-class governance flag was found [S2].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited financial statements, against unaudited nine‑month revenue of {{fact.F40|money}} [S3]
Annual general meeting and dividend decision after a multi‑year zero‑payout record [S2]
Jakarta star‑hotel occupancy and foreign‑arrival data through the mid‑year peak season [S4, S6]

blocks.text: We initiate on JIHD.JK with a HOLD rating and a twelve-month target of Rp320, a -1.4% total return from the last price of Rp324 on 14 November 2026 [S0]. The company owns two Jakarta hotels, an office and retail portfolio in the Sudirman Central Business District (SCBD), a small telecommunications business and a hotel-management arm; PT Kresna Aji Sembada controls 40.0% of the shares [S2]. Market capitalisation is below a trillion rupiah and average daily turnover of IDR233.6m is far under the house floor, so the name fails the liquidity and size screens even though it passes the board test; we state that plainly rather than bury it in a footnote [S0].

The investment case is cash-flow-led, not a sum-of-the-parts claim. At 30 September 2026 total equity was IDR5,067.9bn, of which IDR1,224.9bn was non-controlling interests, leaving parent equity of IDR3,843.0bn; equity-method investments account for IDR1,452.6bn of the balance [S3]. The LK separately appraises land and buildings at IDR6,100.0bn [S3] and discloses an investment-property portfolio in its own note [S3 p.72]. Those appraisals corroborate the asset base but are not a valuation leg: the DCF already capitalises the cash flows from the same properties, so adding their fair value to the bridge would double count, and we publish no NAV. Against a market capitalisation below a trillion rupiah the shares change hands at 0.2x parent book, so the discount to book is not marginal.

Operationally the company is at a trough, not in structural decline. FY2025A revenue was IDR1,612.9bn, essentially flat year on year, with a gross margin of 77.7%; the loss came from operating expenses of IDR1,486.9bn, which included a step-up in real-estate G&A for SCBD maintenance and infrastructure provisions [S2]. Nine-month FY2026 revenue was IDR1,196.2bn and the period produced a net profit only because of a IDR397.7bn non-operating gain that the LK does not break out [S3]; we do not extrapolate it.

Our variant view is that the market is pricing a trough, not a revenue collapse. The reverse DCF at today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 4.4%, slightly below our own FY2027E forecast of 5.0% [S3]; the implied path is consistent with a nine-month run-rate that is broadly flat. We deliberately do not adopt the company's own FY2026 revenue target of IDR1,781.5bn [S2]; we assume the cost base normalises only partially and that EBITDA stays thin until capex tapers. The two things that move the value are the pace of Jakarta occupancy recovery and any transaction that crystallises the property value.

The group reports four segments. In FY2025A real estate earned IDR674.8bn, hotels IDR659.4bn, telecommunication services IDR271.8bn and hotel management IDR6.9bn [S2]. Real estate and hotels therefore generate almost all of the revenue, with telecommunications a distant third and hotel management immaterial to the consolidated total.

The hotel portfolio is small but prime. Hotel Borobudur Jakarta, the larger city hotel, ran at 47.8% room occupancy in FY2025A, while The Ritz-Carlton Pacific Place ran at 84.0% [S2]. Borobudur's occupancy is well below the Jakarta five-star average, which is both the weakness in the current earnings base and the main source of operating leverage if the cycle improves; the Ritz-Carlton asset trades at a premium but has limited room count, so it cannot carry group revenue on its own [S2].

The real-estate arm owns and operates offices and retail space in the SCBD, including the Pacific Place complex, and holds development land at Cibubur [S2]. Its revenue is contractual rent and estate-management fees, with occupancy and rental reversion set by the Jakarta office and retail market rather than by hotel demand. The segment's cost base includes area maintenance, security and infrastructure provisions for the district, which is why real-estate G&A, not hotel costs, drove the FY2025A operating loss [S2].

Strategy is asset management rather than volume growth. The company is investing in the JIHS mixed-use project next to the Borobudur hotel and in SCBD infrastructure; nine-month FY2026 spending on investment properties and property, plant and equipment was substantial relative to revenue, and we expect it to taper once those works complete [S3]. There is no stated plan to sell assets, and no dividend has been paid for several years, so value realisation depends on either a change in capital allocation or a re-rating of the existing assets [S2, S3].

Ownership is concentrated. PT Kresna Aji Sembada has been the controlling shareholder since 2017 with 40.0% of the shares, and the twenty largest holders own 90.2% of the register [S2]. The controlling families also own the affiliated Bank Artha Graha, which holds a large share of the group's cash, and a network of related property and retail businesses that transact with JIHD [S2].

Competitively, JIHD is a niche operator. It is a credible landlord inside the SCBD, where the master-planned district cannot easily be replicated, but it is a small player in Jakarta hotels and a marginal provider of building telecommunications. It is neither the leader nor a challenger in any of its markets; the investment case rests on the cash the properties generate, not on franchise strength, market share, a revaluation of the assets or a narrowing of the discount to parent book, which we do not underwrite [S2].

The SCBD was purpose-built as Jakarta's central business district in the last decade of the twentieth century, and Pacific Place opened a decade later as a luxury retail and hotel complex. Cibubur lies on Jakarta's eastern fringe and has been developed for education and residential use. Indonesia's hotel sector is seasonal, with peak demand around national holidays and the mid-year school break.

Jakarta's hotel market is recovering from a multi-year trough. Statistics Indonesia data reported by Antara put star-hotel occupancy in Jakarta at 58.2% in September 2026, while the national star-hotel occupancy rate was 51.8% in the same month [S4, S7]. Foreign tourist arrivals reached 12.0 m visits in the January to September 2026 period [S6]. Occupancy is still below the levels Jakarta enjoyed before the pandemic, so the recovery has room to run but is not yet strong enough to restore hotel margins to historical levels.

The office and retail market matters as much as hotels, because real estate is the larger segment. Jakarta's central business district has carried elevated office vacancy since the pandemic, with new supply outrunning demand from the technology and financial tenants that absorbed space in the previous cycle [S2]. That caps rental reversion at Pacific Place and the SCBD offices and explains why real-estate revenue has been broadly flat even as hotel occupancy has improved. We assume rent tracks inflation rather than recovering to previous peaks, which is the main reason our revenue growth path is modest [S2, S3].

Domestic policy affects the group through tourism, property and tax channels. Hotel classification, building permits and local hotel and restaurant taxes shape operating costs, while the investment climate for foreign visitors determines corporate and leisure demand [S2]. The annual report notes that the government's medium-term growth target and infrastructure spending support the tourism outlook, but it also flags global trade tensions and financial-market volatility as risks to demand [S2]. We treat policy as a mild tailwind rather than a driver.

Competition in Jakarta luxury hotels is intense. International brands, domestic chains and serviced apartments compete for the same corporate and leisure guests, and buyers have little switching cost, so pricing power is limited outside peak periods. In offices, tenants compare buildings on location, specification and rent, and the SCBD's integrated-district advantage is real but not absolute [S2, S7]. The moat is therefore locational and asset-based rather than commercial: the land cannot be replicated, but the cash flows it produces are exposed to the cycle.

Our five-forces read is unfavourable on most dimensions. Rivalry is high in both hotels and offices; buyer power is high because guests and tenants can switch; supplier power is moderate, with labour, utilities and maintenance contracts the main inputs; the threat of substitutes is moderate, from serviced apartments and from decentralised office locations; and barriers to entry are high for new SCBD-scale districts but low for incremental hotel rooms [S2]. The net effect is that JIHD earns a thin return on its asset base through the cycle and needs either a demand recovery or asset monetisation to create value.

External influences are mostly macro. The rupiah affects inbound tourism and the cost of imported hotel supplies, and Bank Indonesia's policy rate drives the cost of the group's floating-rate bank and lease debt, which stood at IDR577.6bn at 30 September 2026 [S3]. Food and energy prices feed hotel operating costs, but JIHD has no direct commodity exposure and no hedging programme disclosed in the annual report [S2]. Interest rates and the Jakarta cycle, rather than commodity prices, are the variables that matter for our valuation.

Jakarta's office market has been oversupplied for more than a decade, after a wave of new towers was completed just as commodity-driven demand weakened. The city's hotel supply is concentrated in the central business district and around the airport, and international-brand hotels typically operate under management contracts rather than ownership, which is why JIHD's owned-asset model is unusual for its size.

FY2025A revenue was IDR1,612.9bn, -0.7% year on year, with cost of revenue of IDR360.2bn and a gross margin of 77.7% [S2]. The gross margin has been stable for three years, so the swing in profitability came entirely from operating expenses, which rose to IDR1,486.9bn from IDR1,224.7bn a year earlier [S2]. A step-up in real-estate general and administrative costs for SCBD area maintenance and infrastructure provisions accounts for most of that increase, and it took operating profit to IDR-234.2bn [S2].

The nine-month 2026 unaudited LK shows revenue of IDR1,196.2bn, up only marginally year on year, an operating loss of IDR92.9bn, but a net profit of IDR529.5bn after an IDR397.7bn “others – net” gain in the real-estate segment that the LK does not break out [S3 p.3]. The balance sheet at 30 September 2026, restated via facts, reports cash of IDR780.0bn, bank and lease debt of IDR577.6bn, non-controlling interests of IDR1,224.9bn, parent equity of IDR3,843.0bn and equity-method investments of IDR1,452.6bn [S3 pp.1,6]. Total assets were IDR7,500.4bn.

Our forecast builds from the nine-month 2026 run-rate rather than the company’s ambitious IDR1,781.5bn FY2026E target [S2 p.115]; hitting that target would require a jump of more than a third in the fourth quarter, which we deem improbable. We project revenue growth of 3.0% in FY2026E, rising to 4.0% by FY2030E, supported by Jakarta occupancy improvement and arrivals growth. Gross margin is held at the last-actual 77.7%, as hotel and rental revenue is cost-light and the main cost swing has been in G&A. The operating-expense-to-revenue ratio improves from 85.0% in FY2026E to 77.0% by FY2030E, a partial normalisation toward the FY2024A ratio, acknowledging that the FY2025A step-up in real-estate G&A [S2 p.413] will not fully recur.

Depreciation-to-revenue ratio is set at the two-year average of 11.1%, restating the missing D&A in the data pack from facts F9-F10 [S2]. Capex-to-revenue fades from 12.0% in FY2026E, based on the nine-month 2026 spend on investment properties and PP&E [S3], to 11.1% by FY2030E, the three-year maintenance average, as the SCBD and JIHS works complete. Operating working capital remains structurally negative at -38.2% of revenue because of unearned rent, security deposits and accrued infrastructure liabilities [S2].
Earnings-quality flags, run against the house method card:

items: **Accruals**: the accruals ratio ((NI − CFO) / average total assets) is negative in FY2025A and in the forecast years, because cash flow from operations exceeds net income, so earnings are not being inflated by accruals [S2, S3].
**Divergence**: trade receivables fell from the December 2025 level while revenue was broadly flat, so there is no receivables-growth flag [S3].
**IDX regime**: the shares trade on the main board with no special monitoring or notation letters [S0].

**Related parties**: cash and time deposits with affiliated PT Bank Artha Graha Internasional were IDR361.2bn, the majority of group cash [S2 p.421]; related-party liabilities were IDR375.8bn [S2 p.423]; and rental and estate-management revenue from PT Electronic City Indonesia was IDR29.9bn [S2 p.423]. These are established relationships, not aggressive tunnelling.

**Structure**: the controlling shareholder holds 40.0% of the shares [S2]; the free float is 24.5% with average daily turnover of IDR233.6m [S0] — a figure that sits oddly against the 90.2% top-twenty concentration, which caps the tradable float at well under a tenth of the shares, so we use the pack's number only to set the house liquidity discount and flag the discrepancy [S0, S2 p.89]; and no dividend has been paid since at least FY2020 [S2, S3]. No manipulation-class flag is triggered.

blocks.text: Capital allocation: zero dividend payout is assumed throughout the forecast horizon (payout ratio 0.0%) as retained earnings fund the SCBD and JIHS development and maintain the net-cash position [S2, S3]. No net new borrowing is projected. The minority-interest share of net profit is set at 55.0%, the midpoint of the two profitable years FY2023A–FY2024A [S2].

Balance-sheet health: net debt is Rp-190.6bn at FY2026E and Rp-344.1bn at FY2030E - negative, so the group carries net cash that grows as retained cash accumulates [S2, S3]. The net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio is meaningless while EBITDA is negative; once EBITDA turns positive the ratio becomes strongly negative. Equity finances more than half of the balance sheet throughout, a conservative capital structure.

We employ a DCF (FCFF) as the primary valuation method because JIHD is an asset-heavy, capital-intensive operator with negative trailing earnings, making multiple-based benchmarks unreliable. The weighted-average cost of capital of 11.9% is built from a risk-free rate of 7.4% (the ten-year Indonesia government-bond yield), a mature-market equity-risk premium of 4.2%, a country-risk premium of 2.5% for Indonesia, and an industry-default unlevered beta of 0.90. Leveraging with the forecast debt-to-equity ratio of 0.77 produces a levered beta of 1.44, leading to a cost of equity of 15.4% (pre-tax cost of debt 9.4%, tax rate 22.0%). The resulting WACC is applied to the forecast FCFF stream over a ten-year explicit period, with a terminal-value growth rate of 3.5%, below the government's medium-term growth target cited in the annual report [S2]. The terminal value constitutes 51.2% of enterprise value, so the explicit period and the terminal value carry roughly equal weight; the sensitivity grid below shows how far that terminal value moves the answer.

The DCF yields an equity value of Rp351 per share, representing 80.0% of the weighted-average target. The bridge starts from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet: it adds net cash of IDR780.0bn less bank and lease debt of IDR577.6bn, deducts non-controlling interests of IDR1,224.9bn and adds equity-method investments of IDR1,452.6bn [S3]. No post-balance-sheet items are added because the nine-month “others – net” gain of IDR397.7bn [S3] already sits in the investments and equity figures; bridging it again would double count.

Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA is dropped from the weighting entirely rather than carried as a decorative leg, because trailing EBITDA of IDR-48.1bn is negative and any multiple applied to a negative metric returns an economically meaningless value. The P/E method drops out because net profit attributable to the parent is negative through the forecast horizon. Two DCF legs carry the target: the primary five-year DCF at 80% and a DCF to the end of the explicit forecast life with no terminal value at 20% (Rp266 per share, -24.3% versus the primary), which tests the terminal value rather than duplicating it.

**P/BV is a cross-check, not a weighted leg.** At today's 0.2x parent book, P/BV on parent equity of IDR3,843.0bn values the shares close to the DCF, so a leg at the market's current multiple adds little to the target. The own-history mean is roughly twice today's multiple, and carrying it at a quarter of the blend, as the previous draft did, made the entire gap between the DCF and the target depend on a near-doubling of the multiple. We found no source for that re-rating: no dividend since FY2020, no announced asset sale, no stated capital-return policy and no change in the controller or free float that would close the holding-company discount, and parent return on equity stays below the cost of capital through the forecast. We therefore set the leg's weight to zero and disclose the number rather than assert it: at today's multiple the blend sits close to the primary DCF of Rp351, and the final target would be within a few per cent of the share price. If a dividend or a material asset sale at appraised value is announced, the leg becomes live again at a sourced multiple; until then the target rests on cash flow only. The multiple we refuse to underwrite is the stock's own-history mean, not the market's current discount, which is 0.2x today.

Sensitivity analysis: the grid below is the full single-factor map on the DCF. A one-percentage-point move in the WACC or in terminal growth around the base of Rp351 leaves the DCF value inside a narrow band of the base case — the arithmetic is in the table, and the band is modest, not wide, which is why the 51.2% terminal-value share does not dominate the answer. The wider grid is the second table, on the twelve-month target: the operating drivers, revenue growth and gross margin, move the target much further than the discount rate does.

**The compounder card, run on the terminal year.** Terminal capex is set equal to D&A (IDR262.4bn against IDR262.4bn, both 11.1% of revenue), so net fixed-capital reinvestment is nil. The only reinvestment line is operating working capital, which releases IDR-30.5bn as revenue grows against a float of -38.2% of revenue — more than the terminal NOPAT of terminal EBIT IDR16.5bn less tax of IDR2.7bn. The reinvestment rate is therefore negative and the card's g = reinvestment rate × ROIIC identity has no positive-ROIIC solution: the 3.5% terminal growth is not funded by retained capital at all, it is nominal indexation of a cash stream whose growth is paid for by the working-capital float, which is contractual (unearned rent, tenant and project deposits) rather than a financing assumption [S2]. We state that plainly because it is the strongest argument against the terminal value. The forecast roll is not rebased to the 30 September 2026 actual the DCF bridge uses: parent equity is IDR3,411.3bn in the model against IDR3,843.0bn reported at that date [S3], a gap that is almost entirely the unaudited nine-month “others – net” gain of IDR397.7bn and the OCI movement the LK does not break out. We do not bridge that gain into the target a second time, but we do not let it flatter the return test either. Restated on the reported capital — parent equity of IDR3,843.0bn, non-controlling interests of IDR1,224.9bn and net cash of IDR780.0bn less debt of IDR577.6bn [S3] — invested capital is about a tenth higher than the forecast roll, so the terminal-year return on capital is lower than the model shows and far below the 11.9% WACC; the growth is indexation rather than value creation, and the exclusion of the one-off makes the conclusion stronger, not weaker. No explicit fade of returns to the cost of capital is modelled; the fade sits in the operating line, where the opex ratio reaches 77.0% and the EBIT margin 0.7% at the terminal year. The implied exit multiple is the weak point: the terminal value is 51.2% of enterprise value and, against terminal EBIT of IDR16.5bn, implies an exit EV/EBIT of roughly thirty-four times — high because terminal EBIT is thin relative to the cash the float releases. That exit multiple, next to the 51.2% terminal-value share, is why the DCF is the most sensitive leg of the valuation and why the 20.0% discount does not protect the target from a lower terminal multiple. The entry EV/EBIT cannot be computed because FY2025A EBIT was IDR-234.2bn and FY2026E EBIT is IDR-121.3bn; the market currently pays 28.3x current-year EV/EBITDA, a metric that flatters the business because D&A is most of EBITDA. The owner-earnings bridge runs from reported net profit of IDR24.3bn plus D&A of IDR262.4bn less maintenance capex of IDR262.4bn less the working-capital change of IDR-30.5bn, giving owner earnings of IDR54.9bn, of which non-controlling interests take IDR13.4bn.

The reverse DCF is a single-driver sensitivity, not a reading of market psychology. Holding the 11.9% WACC, 3.5% terminal growth and the balance-sheet bridge at base values, the price of Rp324 solves to FY2027E revenue growth of 4.4% against our 5.0% for the same year: the price implies slightly less growth than we forecast, a modest gap, not a decline. It does not carry the 20.0% discount applied to our target, and it moves only one driver, so it is an arithmetic cross-check on our growth path rather than a statement of what the market believes. What it does show is that our revenue path is not heroic: the market's implied FY2027E growth is close to ours, and the gap between our target and the price comes from the DCF's cost of capital and terminal value, not from a bolder revenue forecast and not from a re-rating of the multiple. We read the market's gap to our value as trough-earnings scepticism, not as an expectation of permanent decline [S4, S6].

A 20.0% liquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted target of Rp399 to arrive at the final target of Rp320, acknowledging the thin free float (24.5%) and low average daily turnover (IDR233.6m). The discount is in line with house guidelines for stocks with a free float and turnover below the house thresholds. Without the discount, the target would be Rp399.
**Key downside risks** (ordered by likelihood x impact):

items: **Liquidity and free-float risk** (high likelihood, medium impact): with a 24.5% free float and average daily turnover of IDR233.6m [S0], the stock is illiquid; large block trades can move the price significantly, and exiting a position may prove difficult. The liquidity discount partially mitigates this.

**Occupancy-recovery stall** (medium likelihood, medium impact): Jakarta star-hotel occupancy improved to 58.2% in September 2026 [S4], but a renewed macroeconomic slowdown or fresh travel restrictions could reverse the gain. The hotel segment earned IDR659.4bn of FY2025A revenue [S2]; a five-percentage-point drop in occupancy would flow almost entirely to EBITDA because hotel costs are largely fixed.

**SCBD office-market weakness** (medium likelihood, low impact): Jakarta office vacancy remains elevated, pressuring rental rates and tenant retention [S2]. The real-estate segment earned IDR674.8bn of revenue [S2]; a ten per cent decline in effective rents would reduce group revenue materially.

**Controller-related governance risk** (low likelihood, high impact): the controlling shareholder PT Kresna Aji Sembada (40.0%) could engage in related-party transactions that disadvantage minority shareholders. The current balances (IDR361.2bn at the affiliated bank, IDR29.9bn of rent from Electronic City [S2]) appear stable, but a shift toward aggressive tunnelling would destroy value.

**Interest-rate and FX risk** (low likelihood, low impact): the IDR577.6bn of bank and lease debt [S3] carries a floating-rate component; a rise in Bank Indonesia’s policy rate would raise interest expense. A weaker rupiah would raise the cost of imported hotel supplies, but JIHD’s revenue is mostly rupiah-denominated [S2].

blocks.text: **Bear/base/bull scenarios** mirror the same three drivers — revenue growth, gross margin and the operating-expense ratio — by symmetric shocks, with probabilities of 30%, 45% and 25% respectively. The bear case assumes arrivals growth fades and Jakarta occupancy slips back, SCBD office and retail vacancy keeps real-estate rent flat, and the 2026 cost base does not normalise; the scenario value falls to Rp87 before the 20.0% liquidity discount. The bull case sees foreign arrivals and Jakarta occupancy keep improving, Pacific Place and the SCBD lots re-price with inflation, the Cibubur campus and hotel refurbishments lift revenue, and cost normalisation holds; the scenario value rises to Rp799, again before the 20.0% discount. The base scenario value is Rp386 before the discount, and the probability-weighted target is Rp399 before the discount and Rp320 after it; the weighting does not lean on the bull case, since the weighted value is only modestly above the base.
**Signposts that would change our view**:

items: Quarterly LK filings showing revenue growth consistently below 3.0% would tilt us toward the bear case.
An announced sale of a material SCBD property close to appraised value would move us toward the bull case.
A dividend initiation (none since FY2020) would signal confidence in sustainable cash generation and could reduce the liquidity discount.
A change in auditor or a qualified audit opinion would raise governance flags and possibly trigger a downgrade.

blocks.text: **Ownership and control**: PT Kresna Aji Sembada is the controlling shareholder with a 40.0% stake as of 31 December 2025 [S2 p.90]. The ultimate beneficial owners are the Sugianto Kusuma and Tomy Winata families, who also control PT Bank Artha Graha Internasional and PT Artha Graha Network. The twenty largest shareholders collectively hold 90.2% of outstanding shares, indicating a heavily concentrated ownership structure [S2 p.89]. We found no pledge ('dijaminkan') disclosure in the audited accounts or the annual report [S2].

**Related-party dealings**: JIHD places cash and time deposits with affiliated PT Bank Artha Graha Internasional — IDR361.2bn at FY2025A, the majority of the group’s cash balance [S2 p.421]. Total related-party liabilities were IDR375.8bn [S2 p.423]. The largest component, IDR366.6bn, is a refundable deposit on the Signature Tower project (PT First Jakarta International, related-party note) — a pre-participation operating deposit, not an interest-bearing loan, which is why it does not offset the group’s net cash position [S2 p.404]. Rental and estate-management revenue from PT Electronic City Indonesia amounted to IDR29.9bn in FY2025A [S2 p.423]. These transactions are disclosed at arm’s-length terms in the LK notes, and no unusual patterns suggest tunnelling.

**Auditor and opinion**: The FY2025A financial statements were audited by Kantor Akuntan Publik Osman Bing Satria & Rekan (a member firm of PKF International), which issued an unqualified (“wajar tanpa pengecualian”) opinion [S2 p.338]. The auditor has served since FY2020; no rotation or downgrade has occurred.

**Dividend record**: JIHD has not paid a cash or share dividend since at least FY2020. The FY2024 annual general meeting of shareholders resolved not to distribute a dividend [S2], and the nine-month 2026 retained-earnings balance increased with no distribution [S3]. The payout-ratio forecast is zero throughout our projection horizon.

**Board composition**: The board of directors consists of five members — president director Sugianto Kusuma, director Niko Haryanto, director Adi Septyanto, director Michael A. P. S., and director Danny Kojongian — all of whom are affiliated with the controlling shareholder. The board of commissioners has three members, chaired by Tomy Winata. Independent commissioners hold one seat, below the IDX minimum for independent commissioners, and the LK gives no exemption basis we could verify [S2 p.86]. Governance quality is average for an Indonesian family-controlled listed entity.

**ESG exposures**: Environmental — hotel operations consume energy and water, and generate waste; JIHD reports certification of its environmental-management system and mentions initiatives to reduce energy consumption and plastic waste [S2 p.58–59]. Social — the company employs 1,906 people, with labour-relations practices typical for the hospitality sector. Governance — the concentrated ownership and below-par independent-commissioner representation are weaknesses, but there is no history of regulatory sanctions or shareholder activism [S2].
**Dated catalysts** (also listed in the frontmatter):

items: **FY2026 audited LK publication** (expected 31 March 2027). The unaudited nine-month 2026 LK showed revenue of IDR1,196.2bn [S3]; the full-year audited figures will confirm whether the company met its IDR1,781.5bn target or, as we expect, fell short. A revenue figure close to our forecast of IDR1,661.2bn would support our base case.

**SCBD occupancy and rental-rate updates** (May–July 2027). Following the investment in property and PP&E during the nine months to September 2026 [S3], the SCBD portfolio’s occupancy and effective rents will show whether the capex is yielding the intended returns. Property-consultancy reports will serve as a proxy.

**Reference-rate reset** (1 July 2027). A portion of the IDR577.6bn bank debt is floating-rate; the reset will update the cost-of-debt assumption (currently 9.4% pre-tax) and could affect net interest expense materially [S3].

blocks.text: **Key performance indicators to monitor** between updates [S2, S3]:

items: **Quarterly revenue** — compare with our forecast of IDR1,661.2bn for FY2026E and IDR1,744.3bn for FY2027E [S3]. A consistent miss of more than five per cent would trigger a forecast review.
**Jakarta star-hotel occupancy** — track monthly BPS releases; our model assumes occupancy stabilises around 58.2% and gradually improves. A drop below fifty-five per cent would be a negative signal.

**Net-cash position** — monitor cash less debt in each LK; our forecast shows net debt of Rp-190.6bn in FY2026E and Rp-344.1bn in FY2030E. A material draw-down that turns the position positive would indicate financial stress.
**SCBD rental collections** — watch for any mention of tenant defaults or rent concessions in the MD&A of quarterly LKs; our real-estate revenue forecast assumes stable collections.
**Related-party balances** — scrutinise any increase in cash placed at PT Bank Artha Graha Internasional beyond the IDR361.2bn level, or new related-party loans not disclosed in the notes.

blocks.text: **Events that would prompt an update** before the scheduled six-monthly refresh [S2, S3]:

items: A material asset sale (for example a SCBD plot) at a price significantly different from the appraised IDR6,100.0bn [S3].
A change in controlling shareholder or a large block trade that alters the free-float percentage.
A dividend declaration (unlikely given the historical record).
A qualified audit opinion or auditor change.
A regulatory action (special monitoring board status or a Bapepam-LK investigation).

blocks.text: We will review the JIHD position quarterly, coinciding with LK filings, and will publish an update if any of the above events materially affects the investment thesis or valuation [S2].

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is set at +3.0% yoy, a little above the annualised 9M 2026 run-rate on a seasonally stronger Q4, and far below the company's Rp1,781.5bn target: revenue of Rp1,196.2bn in 9M 2026 was only +0.7% yoy, so hitting the target would need +38% in Q4. We grow FY2026E +3.0%, then 5.0/5.0/4.5/4.0% as Jakarta star-hotel occupancy (58.18% in September 2026, +5.15pp yoy) and arrivals (12.01m to September, +5.01%) support a gradual recovery, with the company's target as the upside case rather than the base.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A actual gross margin 77.7% (Rp1,252.7bn on Rp1,612.9bn revenue); FY2024A 78.1% and FY2023A 78.4%. Held at the last actual with no recovery or erosion assumed: hotel and rental revenue is cost-light and the main cost swing has been in G&A, not cost of revenues.

assumptions.label: SG&A and final tax / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E starts from the 9M 2026 actual: opex of Rp1,029.2bn on revenue of Rp1,196.2bn, 86.0% (92.2% in FY2025A, 75.4% in FY2024A, 75.0% in FY2023A). The 2025 increase is documented in note 33 (G&A Rp1,114.7bn to Rp1,374.8bn, of which real estate Rp616.2bn to Rp813.8bn, p.412) but the MD&A gives no permanent driver for it. A ratio above the 77.7% gross margin would leave EBIT negative in perpetuity, which is not a going concern; we converge to 77.0% by FY2030E, still 1.6pp above the last normal year (FY2024A), so only part of the 2025 step-up is assumed to reverse.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total D&A from the LK notes (PP&E plus investment-property depreciation) was Rp186.1bn in FY2025A and Rp172.6bn in FY2024A, i.e. 11.5% and 10.6% of revenue; 11.1% is the two-year average. The pack carries no D&A, so history is restated from facts F9/F10.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E follows the current investment programme: 9M 2026 spend of Rp207.9bn on investment properties (Rp164.8bn) and PP&E (Rp43.1bn) is ~13% of annualised revenue. It fades to 9/7/5.5% as the SCBD and JIHS works complete, then to the 11.1% necessary to match terminal D&A at 3.5% growth, consistent with a going‑concern hotel‑and‑property owner (the house method card).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital is structurally negative because of unearned rent, security deposits and accrued infrastructure liabilities; FY2025A was -Rp675.9bn, or -38.2% of revenue, and the three-year average is held.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2024A effective income tax was 10.8% of pre-tax profit (Rp36.3bn on Rp335.6bn); the final tax on revenue is already inside operating expenses, so the 10% cash tax rate on positive pre-tax profit is held.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default: FY2025A interest expense over opening debt (8.9%); the LK shows bank facilities at 8-11%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default: FY2025A interest income over opening cash (3.9%); most cash sits in time deposits at the affiliated bank.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero net new borrowing assumed: FY2025A debt was Rp198.2bn and 9M 2026 drawings lifted bank and lease debt to Rp577.6bn, which we capture in the 30 September balance sheet rather than project further; no refinancing or repayment is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Set to zero: the recurring Rp260.4bn rental and estate-management income and the associates' share of profit sit below operating profit in the LK and are not projected; the 9M 2026 Rp397.7bn 'others - net' is a one-off that is not extrapolated.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 58.7% of FY2024A net profit (Rp175.7bn of Rp299.2bn) and 75.4% in FY2023A; 2025 is not usable because the parent booked the loss while minorities stayed profitable. 55% is the mid-point of the two profitable years and is applied to forecast net profit.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid since at least FY2020; the FY2024 AGMS resolved not to distribute a cash or share dividend, and the 9M 2026 retained earnings rose with no distribution. Zero payout through the forecast horizon.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No corporate action changed the 2,329,040,482 shares outstanding in 2025; zero assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.5% long-run nominal growth, below the government's 5.4% 2026 growth target cited in the AR and consistent with a mature Jakarta hotel and rental portfolio; the terminal value is a little over half of enterprise value, so the sensitivity table tests a 1pp range.
